title: [Amazon AWS] Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg
summary: Today, we’re announcing a simple, cost-effective path for data lake modernization. Amazon S3 Tables now support managed migration of your Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg. Migration works with Parquet tables in Amazon S3 that are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and allows you to upgrade your data lake with no pipelines to build or compute to provision, while production workloads keep running. Apache Iceberg has become the open standard for large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data open and queryable with any Iceberg-compatible engine. Amazon S3 Tables offer fully managed storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with features like automatic maintenance, optimization, replication, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering built-in. What is new Previously, migrating Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg could take weeks of engineering work to build and manage the required infrastructure. Converting data types and building rollback capabilities added operational complexity. Now, this is available as a managed, API-driven operation. S3 Tables handle the entire migration workflow, including data validation, compatibility checks, type conversions, file recompression, and compaction. Before copying any data, S3 Tables identify every source object in scope and generate a compatibility report. You can sync as many times as you need without stopping writes to your source table, except for a few minutes during cutover. Once you are ready, you can complete the migration, minimizing time that tables are offline. Compared to self-managed approaches, S3 Tables managed migrations are cost-effective because you pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the Hive-to-Iceberg conversion, and source objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering stay in their current access tier. A first look at the migration To migrate an AWS Glue Hive table, choose your destination table bucket in the S3 console, then choose Create table from migration. Create a namespace and table name for your destination Iceberg table. The destination table is created using recommended default settings tuned for query performance and storage efficiency. When you start the migration, S3 Tables validate the source table, generate a compatibility report, and begin copying data. The destination table is read-only during the migration. Once you complete migration, the destination table is promoted to read-write. You can begin working with your data right away using a direct integration with Amazon Athena and Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio in the AWS console, or use any tool compatible with the Apache Iceberg REST API to directly query the tables. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables migration documentation. You can also use AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, or the Agent Toolkit for AWS. For example, set up migration jobs and call the start-table-migration command. cat > /tmp/start-migration.json <<'EOF' { "roleARN": "arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/S3TablesMigrationRole", "destinationTable": { "tableBucketARN": "arn:aws:s3tables:us-east-1:123456789012:bucket/my-destination-bucket", "namespace": "mynamespace", "name": "my_destination_table", "encryptionConfiguration": { "sseAlgorithm": "aws:kms", "kmsKeyArn": "arn:aws:kms:us-east-1:123456789012:key/1234abcd-12ab-34cd-56ef-1234567890ab" }, "storageClassConfiguration": { "storageClass": "INTELLIGENT_TIERING" }, "tags": { "team": "s3tables", "purpose": "migration" }, "properties": { "writeFormat": "parquet", "icebergFormatVersion": 2, "compressionCodec": "zstd", "dictionaryEncoding": true }, "schema": { "type": "struct", "schemaId": 0, "identifierFieldIds": , "fields":  }, "icebergSortOrder": { "orderId": 1, "fields":  } }, "sourceType": "glueTable", "source": { "glueTable": { "catalogId": "123456789012", "databaseName": "my_glue_database", "tableName": "my_source_table" } }, "dataMigration": { "maintenanceSettings": { "icebergCompaction": { "targetFileSizeMB": 512, "strategy": "binpack" }, "icebergSnapshotManagement": { "minSnapshotsToKeep": 3, "maxSnapshotAgeHours": 168 } }, "migrationPolicies": { "unmatchedSourceFieldsPolicy": "fail", "incompatibleValuesPolicy": "fail" } }, "reviewMigrationPlan": false, "migrationOutput": { "bucket": "arn:aws:s3:::my-report-bucket", "prefixes": { "tableCompatibilityReport": "reports/table-compatibility/", "objectCompatibilityReport": "reports/object-compatibility/", "objectMigrationReport": "reports/object-migration/" } } } EOF aws s3tables start-table-migration \ --cli-input-json file:///tmp/start-migration.json To catch up the destination table with changes in the source, call sync-table-migration as many times as you need before you complete the migration. Each sync copies only what changed. If you’re using coding agents like Kiro, the migrating-hive-tables-to-s3-tables skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS provides step-by-step migration guidance with safety guardrails for agents. The skill can: Analyze existing IAM policies and recommend equivalent destination policies Validate the migration plan before getting started Execute the Start → Sync → Complete API calls Monitor job progress and guide validation and cutover To learn more, visit the GitHub README page for the skill. Now available Amazon S3 Tables managed migration is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), and Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, Stockholm) Regions. At launch, the capability supports AWS Glue-registered Hive tables stored in Parquet format within the same AWS account and AWS Region. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, or troubleshoot about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool. Try it in the Amazon S3 console today and send feedback to AWS re:Post for Amazon S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts. — Channy

title: [Amazon AWS] AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026)
summary: The agentic launches that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is. They were about reach. AWS Step Functions, which already orchestrates over 220 AWS services, can now be handed to an agent as a tool, so workflows teams already trust became callable without a rewrite. In the same week, the AI blog published how one engagement platform exposed roughly 400 internal API operations the same way. Neither story involves rebuilding anything, only describing what exists and letting the agent find it. The other thread was cost. OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum launches landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news… Headlines OpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops. Terra is the everyday-workload line of the GPT-6 family. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than both. Those are OpenAI’s figures, not an independent test. The price is what I would check first: input and output tokens are at least 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It takes up to 1 million input tokens with text and image input, and you can reach it from the Bedrock APIs or ChatGPT Work and Codex. AWS Step Functions workflows are now available as AI agent tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which connects agents to tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The division of labor is the idea: the agent decides when to run a workflow and what input to pass; Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. A support agent can trigger a refund, and the eligibility check, the manager approval, and the credit still happen in that order every time, because the ordering was never the model’s to improvise. Your existing Standard and Express workflows qualify as connector targets, and agents can also look up runs. It’s available in all Regions where AgentCore Gateway is, at standard rates. Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention: AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation – You can now establish a shared secret with a post-quantum algorithm using AWS KMS keys, with private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. All three NIST FIPS 203 parameter sets are supported through Encapsulate, which produces a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext, and Decapsulate, which recovers it. The threat is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records today’s key exchange and recovers the secret once quantum computers are powerful enough. It’s available everywhere KMS runs except the Middle East (UAE and Bahrain) and China Regions. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL added post-quantum TLS key exchange the same week, on versions 18 and higher. AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation – You can now carry a user’s identity with their request to AWS services in another Region. This removes a genuine architectural constraint: trusted identity propagation used to require every service accessing that identity to sit in the same Region, which left two unappealing options, broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual users, or consolidating all your services into a single Region. Now the identity travels with the request automatically, so you grant access by user and group membership and audit who accessed what. It’s available at no additional cost everywhere IAM Identity Center runs. Amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) – You can now run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU, the practical answer to work that only ever uses a fraction of one, like small-model inference and multi-model serving. You declare the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally cap its share of GPU compute, and ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale, with no code changes. It works on ECS Managed Instances and ECS on Amazon EC2, and on Managed Instances it watches the MPS control daemon and replaces the instance if it turns unhealthy. It’s available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances – You can now have AWS Lambda fetch only the files needed at each stage of startup instead of pulling a whole container image first, which AWS puts at up to 70% off container startup time. You create a SOCI index, push it to Amazon ECR, point the image URI at the indexed tag, and Lambda detects it automatically. The technique also reached Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs, with benchmarks: lazy loading held at 3 to 11 seconds regardless of image size, against a median 3 minutes 42 seconds for a 13.2 GB image, a range they report as 8x to 46x. Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API – You can now declare how traffic reaches your applications with Gateway and HTTPRoute resources on Amazon EKS without installing a separate controller, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS load balancing infrastructure. You get HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace routing, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager. Existing Ingress workloads keep working alongside them, so this is additive rather than a migration. Gateway API support is included with EKS Auto Mode; standard load balancing charges apply. For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page. Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting: How Nubank automated disaster recovery with the AWS DevOps Agent – Nubank serves more than 140 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, and classifies over 300 business flows as critical, each tested on a regulator’s schedule. Nubank reports that handing evidence collection and report writing to the AWS DevOps Agent cut a test cycle from about 4.3 hours to roughly 40 minutes, and quadrupled flow coverage in 2026 to more than 160. One execution terminated more than 900 EKS instances under synthetic traffic with AWS Fault Injection Service, producing the evidence its regulator needed. How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway – Roughly 400 internal REST API operations, built by 25 teams, sitting in private VPCs across seven Regions, with tenant identity that could never become a parameter the model gets to set. MoEngage estimates the managed path saved about six months of platform engineering. The detail worth stealing: a full tool listing would have crossed 20,000 tokens per connection, so agents search for tools by describing a task instead of receiving the catalog. Reducing petabyte-scale S3 storage costs with evidence-based lifecycle rules – The hard part isn’t deciding to act, it’s knowing which data has gone cold and where it can safely live. This uses S3 Storage Lens groups and Storage Class Analysis to prove access patterns before moving anything. In the engagement described, 5.8 PB of logs in Amazon S3 Standard at approximately $241,000 per month showed an access ratio below 0.1% past 90 days, and a 90-day transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cut the bill by roughly 70%, a figure the author ties to that workload. Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events: AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, with more than 2,200 sessions. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up. AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders. The 2026 season is winding down as re:Invent approaches, so check the hub for what’s still on. Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events. That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup! – Daniel Abib This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

title: [Amazon AWS] Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services
summary: When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every new service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs), AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, update, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization. Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account. ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams. Platform teams create and configure a gateway, defining organizational networking standards including subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and WAF web ACLs, in a single place. They then associate the gateway with one or more ECS clusters, making it available to services running on those clusters. Application teams opt their services in by adding a gateway connector parameter when creating or updating a service. ECS provisions the required per-service resources automatically: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, target groups, and a service security group that permits inbound traffic only from the ALB. No networking expertise required. ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes. A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later. Choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation. Using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector. aws ecs create-gateway \ --name my-team-gateway \ --infrastructure-role-arn arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ECSGatewayRole \ --configuration '{ "HostSharedAlb": { "networkConfiguration": { "subnets": , "ipAddressType": "ipv4" }, "scheme": "internet-facing" } }' Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters. Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters. Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster: aws ecs associate-gateway-with-cluster \ --gateway my-team-gateway \ --cluster arn:aws:ecs:us-east-1:123456789012:cluster/my-cluster To create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Gateway documentation. ECS Gateway:Behind the scenes A gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster. Platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters. Application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in CreateService or UpdateService. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling UpdateService to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration. aws ecs create-service \ --cluster my-cluster \ --service my-api-service \ --task-definition my-api-service:1 \ --gateway-connectors '}, "healthCheck": {...} }]' At deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets. For each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a new one (up to maxAlbCount referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes ACTIVE, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic. ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically: Redeployments: On each deployment, ECS re-evaluates gateway associations. If new compatible gateways have been associated since the last deployment, your service connects to them. If a gateway has been disassociated, your service disconnects and the route is removed. Your service always reflects the current state of the cluster gateways at deployment time. Service deletion: ECS automatically disconnects the service from every gateway, removes all gateway routes, and cleans up all per-service resources. If the service held the last route on an ALB, that ALB is deprovisioned. Things to Know Here are a few important details to keep in mind: Networking: ECS Gateway is available for ECS services using the awsvpc network mode across all launch types (Amazon ECS EC2, AWS Fargate, and ECS Managed Instances). Your service Availability Zones (AZs) must be a subset of each gateway’s AZs on the cluster. A gateway ALB only routes traffic to tasks in AZs where it has subnets. We recommend creating gateways and services for a given cluster with the same set of AZs. Capacity: If maxAlbCount is reached and no ALB has available capacity, the deployment fails. Default quota limit of maxAlbCount is 10. Plan your maxAlbCount setting according to the number of services you expect to connect. Observability: Use ALB metrics in CloudWatch with the TargetGroup dimension to monitor per-service traffic, and LoadBalancer dimension to monitor traffic across the shared ALB. Use describe-target-health to check real-time target status. Configure CloudWatch alarms for metrics such as HealthyHostCount, TargetResponseTime, and HTTPCode_Target_5XX_Count, using gateway ARN-based tagging so monitoring scales automatically with your maxAlbCount. Now available Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Pricing page. To get started, create your first gateway today in the ECS console, and send feedback to AWS re:Post for ECS or through your usual AWS Support contacts. — Channy

title: [HashiCorp] Building Self-Service into Terraform: Introducing Terraform Developer Portal (Public Preview)
summary: Terraform has long helped platform teams standardize how infrastructure is provisioned and managed. As Terraform adoption grows across an organization, the next challenge is making that infrastructure easier for developers to consume. Developers shouldn't need to understand every Terraform module, workspace, or organizational standard before they can get the infrastructure they need. At the same time, platform teams need to maintain control over what gets provisioned and how. We're investing in making self-service a native part of the Terraform experience. That means giving developers a simpler way to discover and consume approved infrastructure, while giving platform teams the controls they need to define and govern those experiences. Increasingly, it also means making that same self-service foundation available to AI agents. Terraform Developer Portal: a native self-service experience for developers Terraform Developer Portal (TDP), provides a native self-service experience for developers to discover, provision, and manage infrastructure through Terraform. Platform teams can expose existing Terraform modules as curated Templates, defining the inputs developers need to provide while maintaining control over how infrastructure is provisioned. For example, a platform team might expose an approved AWS module as a Template such as Create an Application Service. Developers select the Template, provide the required inputs, and Terraform handles the underlying provisioning. The resulting infrastructure is represented as an Application, which developers can extend with approved Add-ons, such as a PostgreSQL database. Terraform Actions provide approved operational workflows beyond initial provisioning. Together, Templates, Applications, Add-ons, and Actions give developers a simpler way to consume and manage infrastructure while Terraform remains the underlying provisioning engine. Agentic self-service: bringing Terraform self-service to agents The way developers interact with infrastructure is also changing. Today, a developer might open a UI or use a CLI to provision infrastructure. Increasingly, they may simply describe what they need to an AI agent. For example: Create a development application for the payments service and add a PostgreSQL database. An agent could discover the approved infrastructure available to that developer, identify the appropriate Template, determine its required inputs, and initiate the same provisioning workflow available through TDP. Or a developer might ask: What infrastructure does the payments application have, and did the latest provisioning run succeed? Instead of requiring the developer to navigate through multiple infrastructure resources, an agent could retrieve the relevant application and Terraform context and provide an answer. The same approach can extend to other self-service workflows: Add the approved database Add-on to my application. Show me the available infrastructure I can provision. Why did my infrastructure provisioning fail? Run an approved Action against my application. The important part of agentic self-service is that the agent doesn't bypass the platform team's existing controls. Agents operate through the same Terraform APIs and workflows, discovering and consuming infrastructure that platform teams have already made available through self-service. Capabilities such as tfctl provide a way for humans, automation, and coding agents to interact with Terraform programmatically. MCP can further make Terraform context and self-service capabilities discoverable to agents. This creates a model where UI, CLI, API, and agents are different interfaces into the same Terraform self-service foundation, rather than separate ways of managing infrastructure. A broader self-service direction for Terraform Terraform Developer Portal establishes the foundation for developer self-service. Platform teams define approved infrastructure and workflows, while developers get a simpler way to discover, provision, and manage them. Agentic self-service extends that model by allowing developers to access the same capabilities through the tools and agents where they increasingly work. The underlying model remains the same. Platform teams define the infrastructure, workflows, permissions, and organizational standards. Terraform manages infrastructure provisioning and lifecycle. Developers choose what they need without having to understand all of the implementation details underneath. Whether a developer starts from the TDP UI, CLI, API, or an AI agent, our direction is the same. We want to make the infrastructure organizations already manage with Terraform easier to discover and consume without sacrificing the control platform teams need. title: [HashiCorp] Announcing the public preview of HashiCorp Secure Hub: Govern Vault at scale
summary: HashiCorp Vault has become a critical security platform for organizations managing secrets, credentials, certificates, cryptographic services, and machine and agentic access across hybrid and multi-cloud environments. As adoption expands to more applications, teams, business units, and regions, however, organizations face a new challenge: understanding and governing their growing Vault estate as a whole. What can be managed effectively within individual environments becomes increasingly complex as organizations need to understand operational health, security resources, usage, and lifecycle activity at enterprise scale. Today, we are announcing the public preview of HashiCorp Secure Hub, a common governance layer that gives organizations a unified way to understand and govern their Vault estate. Secure Hub brings together visibility, reporting, and operational context from distributed Vault environments, giving platform, security, and governance teams a more complete view of the security resources they manage. Secure Hub complements the security controls and enforcement within Vault Enterprise rather than replacing them. Vault continues to secure and enforce access within individual environments, while Secure Hub provides the enterprise-wide context needed to govern the broader Vault estate. Together, they enable organizations to maintain distributed security controls while establishing more consistent visibility and governance at enterprise scale. Extending the value of Vault Enterprise Organizations often expand Vault usage organically as more teams and applications adopt secrets management, PKI, and other security services. Over time, that success can result in multiple Vault environments supporting different applications, regions, or organizational requirements. Secure Hub brings these environments into a common governance experience without changing the role Vault plays in securing individual workloads. It gives teams a consolidated way to understand the health, security resources, activity, and consumption of their Vault estate with capabilities such as: Centralized visibility. Establish a consolidated view of Vault environments, including information about cluster operational health, configuration, and versions, to help platform teams better understand and operate their Vault estate. Improved secrets reporting. Gain greater visibility into the types of secrets that exist in different environments when they were modified or used, and other information that can help teams monitor security practices and respond to governance or audit requirements. Improved certificate reporting. Greater visibility into issued and expiring certificates throughout the Vault estate, helping teams identify upcoming lifecycle events and coordinate renewal activities. Consistent governance across environments. Establish enterprise-wide visibility and governance while preserving the policies, controls, and enforcement appropriate to each Vault environment. Licensing consumption visibility. Track Resource Unit consumption by cluster and namespace to improve usage visibility and predictability. Build on the Vault investments you have today Secure Hub is designed to deliver value for organizations operating Vault Enterprise today. Customers can build on their existing deployments and operating models while gaining additional reporting and governance capabilities across teams, regions, and use cases. Secure Hub is also designed to support Vault Arc, providing continuity as organizations introduce the new generation of Vault alongside their existing environments. This creates a path toward consistent governance of Vault Enterprise and Vault Arc as the portfolio evolves. Vault Arc, however, is not a prerequisite for Secure Hub. Organizations can begin realizing the value of Secure Hub with the Vault Enterprise environments they operate today. Expanding Security Lifecycle Management Security Lifecycle Management requires organizations to understand not only individual secrets, certificates, and cryptographic assets, but how those resources are created, used, governed, and ultimately retired through the enterprise. As Vault adoption expands, that lifecycle increasingly spans teams, environments, regions, and generations of Vault. Secure Hub expands SLM from managing security resources within individual environments toward governing their lifecycle in the enterprise. That becomes increasingly important as machine identities proliferate and organizations adopt agentic AI, creating more identities, credentials, certificates, and access relationships that must be understood and governed at scale. Together, Vault Enterprise, Vault Arc, Secure Hub, and capabilities from the broader IBM security portfolio can provide a foundation for discovering, securing, and governing human, machine, workload, and agentic access in increasingly autonomous environments. The public preview gives customers an opportunity to experience this new approach to governing Vault at enterprise scale and provide feedback that helps shape the evolution of Secure Hub. As Vault estates continue to expand and security lifecycles become more distributed, that feedback will help define how Secure Hub evolves to meet the governance needs of increasingly complex and autonomous environments. Join the HashiCorp Secure Hub public preview to explore the new capabilities, share your feedback, and evaluate how Vault Arc can extend your organization's Security Lifecycle Management strategy. Learn more about the SLM announcements at TechXchange.

title: [CNCF] Faster LLM inference startup: What you need to know
summary: Adding an inference replica creates capacity only after the new instance can serve requests. Between starting a process and generating a response, an LLM server may need to load weights, initialize GPU resources, compile kernels, capture execution graphs, and warm up the engine. Restarts, model switches, and scale-out can repeat this work. The community is addressing these costs at several levels. vLLM and SGLang are developing ways to reuse weights and initialized state. Serving platforms are building workflows around warm instances and snapshots. Kubernetes, container runtimes, and the Open Container Initiative (OCI) are working on related interfaces and artifact questions. These efforts have different boundaries and are progressing independently. Understanding what each approach preserves helps explain both its benefits and its current scope. Why starting an inference server takes time A typical startup includes several kinds of work. The server launches processes and imports libraries. It reads model files, constructs tensors, and performs any required weight transformations. It initializes the execution runtime and communication between workers, allocates memory, and prepares the engine to serve. Some work happens specifically to improve subsequent inference performance. Compilation produces executable kernels; autotuning selects implementations for a configuration. CUDA Graph capture records GPU operations for later replay with lower launch overhead. The vLLM optimization documentation describes the tradeoff between startup work and steady-state execution performance. The balance depends on the model, software, hardware, and storage. Once model files are cached locally, engine initialization may become more visible. Once weights can be reused in GPU memory, imports, tuning, and graph capture may account for more of the remaining delay. What can be reused instead of rebuilt Startup optimizations can be grouped by the work they preserve: What is reusedApproachRepresentative projects or featuresWork that can remainModel filesPre-staging and efficient loadersllm-d model caches, fastsafetensorsWeight processing and initializationCompiled artifacts and tuning resultsPersistent cachesvLLM compilation and autotune cachesRuntime setup and graph captureProcessed weightsDaemons and weight transfervLLM preload, SGLang weight cache, ModelExpressConstruction of the rest of the engineA live engineSleep/wake and warm instancesvLLM sleep, SGLang memory saver, llm-d FMARestoring released resourcesInitialized execution stateEngine or container snapshotsvLLM snapshots, SGLang snapshot proposal, Snapshot, llm-d/GKEValidation, restoration, and recovery work These approaches can appear together in a system, with integration conditions specific to each implementation. For example, an engine might reuse compiled artifacts while loading weights through a specialized loader. A snapshot workflow might discard an empty key/value (KV) cache before capture and recreate it after restoration. This cache holds attention state computed while processing tokens. Efficient loading remains a separate area of work. SGLang documents loaders such as pre-sharded state, fastsafetensors, and streaming loaders. llm-d documents model-file caches alongside other startup paths. These mechanisms affect how weights reach an engine; they preserve different states from a snapshot of an initialized process. SGLang model loading, llm-d startup overview. What vLLM and SGLang are doing vLLM vLLM’s Fast Start work centers on a persistent weight daemon. It loads and processes weights, holds the resulting tensors in GPU memory, and exposes them to compatible engines through CUDA inter-process communication. The weight-daemon implementation and the vllm preload command have been merged. Current preload documentation also describes preparing FlashInfer autotune results before an engine starts. Fast Start implementation, preload documentation. This separates the lifetime of cached weights from an engine restart. In the zero-copy mode, an engine maps the daemon’s existing allocations. Configuration checks determine whether reuse is appropriate, and the documented path can fall back to ordinary loading. The daemon must remain alive while engines use its memory. CUDA IPC handles are local to a node; documented multi-node deployments provide the relevant shards locally on each node. vLLM also has sleep/wake support, which retains a live server while releasing much of its GPU memory. That provides a different lifecycle from starting a new engine against cached weights. The preload documentation identifies restrictions on combining its zero-copy mode with weight offloading through sleep mode. Sleep mode. A separate, merged implementation adds experimental initialized-engine snapshots. The vllm snapshot workflow uses CRIU to capture and restore Linux process state, with CUDA checkpoint support handling GPU state. Its documented scope requires the same machine and compatible environment, with one NVIDIA GPU and tensor parallelism of one. It releases weights and KV state before capture and reloads them during restoration, retaining a dependency on the model files. Restoration also checks a recorded generation result. Initialized engine snapshots. SGLang SGLang has merged a weight-cache daemon that holds processed weights and shares them with new engine instances through CUDA IPC. Its Fast Engine Recovery roadmap discusses extending this foundation, including broader model and quantization coverage, memory transport, daemon lifecycle, and remaining initialization costs. The roadmap describes directions beyond the merged initial implementation. Weight-cache implementation, Fast Engine Recovery roadmap. SGLang also exposes memory release/resume and generation pause/continue operations used by external snapshot integrations. Whether weights remain available after release depends on the configured memory policy, including CPU backup. These operations let integrations prepare an engine for capture and resume it afterward; the surrounding workflow still needs to coordinate them. Initialized-engine snapshots are another direction. The open RFC and implementation PR propose capturing SGLang after initialization and before its HTTP service binds. Their initial scope is one NVIDIA GPU, tensor parallelism of one, and the same host and software environment. Model weights remain external and are reloaded after restore. Initialization snapshot RFC, implementation PR. Both frameworks also have open proposals about cooperating with an external checkpoint orchestrator. The engine would prepare its own state and resume serving; the external system would capture, store, and restore the process. These proposals address a practical boundary: a node agent can operate checkpoint tools, while the inference engine knows when its requests, caches, and communication resources are safe to capture. vLLM proposal, SGLang proposal. How platforms turn mechanisms into startup workflows Snapshot and Dynamo The independent Snapshot project in the ai-dynamo organization provides checkpoint and restore primitives for GPU workloads on Kubernetes. Its operator and node agent coordinate CRIU and CUDA checkpoint operations, with resources such as PodSnapshot and SnapshotJob. Dynamo integrates these primitives into its serving workflows. Snapshot project. Snapshot’s documented storage path uses a shared persistent volume accessible by node agents. Agent-side components manage artifact movement and restore access. Its current storage documentation supports storage through a Kubernetes PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC); object-storage backends are reserved for future use. Hardware, driver, runtime, and workload compatibility still constrain restoration. Storage model. The framework examples also show the application work involved. The SGLang example mounts an entrypoint that warms the engine, pauses generation, releases memory, and signals that capture is safe. After restoration, it resumes memory and generation, validates a generation, and starts its API. The vLLM guide validates its own entrypoint on v0.27.1 and explicitly says that example does not work on v0.28. This illustrates a compatibility boundary for that integration. SGLang guide, vLLM guide. Dynamo separately develops GPU Memory Service, which moves GPU-memory ownership outside the engine process. Its integration and snapshot support need to be read by version: Dynamo’s v1.4.0 Snapshot documentation explicitly describes GMS plus Snapshot as disabled and unsupported for production. GPU Memory Service, versioned Snapshot documentation. llm-d llm-d documents several startup approaches. Its Pod Snapshots guide currently covers single-GPU vLLM and SGLang deployments using GKE Pod Snapshots, GKE Sandbox based on gVisor, and Google Cloud Storage. The initial instance loads and warms the model, prepares its memory, and triggers a snapshot. Compatible later Pods restore that state and resume the framework. The guide describes a platform-independent CRIU backend as work in progress. Pod Snapshots guide. This backend differs from Snapshot’s CRIU path. gVisor saves sandbox state through its own checkpoint mechanism; GKE documents GPU-state capture through NVIDIA checkpoint support. Similar high-level workflows therefore do not imply identical checkpoint formats or APIs. GKE Pod snapshots. Fast Model Actuation takes another approach. It uses controllers and a requester/launcher Pod arrangement to manage vLLM instances. Depending on available state and placement, it can wake a sleeping instance or start one through a launcher that has already loaded Python modules. Its hot path depends on matching the retained instance to the assigned GPU. FMA guide. llm-d also documents ModelExpress for transferring weights from a seed replica to peers using NIXL and remote direct memory access (RDMA) over a compatible network. This changes weight distribution while leaving other engine-startup work to the receiving instance. These three paths illustrate why a platform’s startup work cannot be represented by a single checkpoint feature. ModelExpress integration. Where Kubernetes checkpoint and restore stands The Kubernetes Checkpoint Restore Working Group provides a place to coordinate use cases, API proposals, and integration with SIGs and runtimes. Its charter also identifies checkpoint archive efficiency as an area to revisit. The group’s scope concerns platform orchestration; inference frameworks continue to develop their internal startup mechanisms independently. Working-group charter. Kubernetes already has container checkpointing through the work associated with Kubernetes Enhancement Proposal (KEP) 2008, which reached beta in v1.30. KEP-5823 addresses Pod-level checkpoint and restore. It is marked implementable with a v1.38 alpha target; that milestone is a delivery target. Its initial boundaries exclude device state and cross-node restore. GPU support has a separate provisional proposal, KEP-6274, whose enhancement PR remains open and discusses device allocation and compatibility. Container checkpoint API, Pod-level proposal, GPU proposal. There is concrete progress at the Container Runtime Interface, or CRI, boundary. The PR adding CheckpointPod and RestorePod merged on July 22, 2026. The current interface describes consistent capture, resumption after checkpointing, and cleanup on restore failure. Restore prepares containers before their execution starts. The Kubernetes orchestration and containerd implementation PRs remain open; CRI-O’s implementation PR is a draft. CRI API change, Kubernetes implementation, containerd implementation, CRI-O implementation. CRI leaves checkpoint files and their layout to the runtime. OCI addresses a different concern: packaging and distribution. Its image specification supports generic artifacts, and its distribution specification provides registry transfer and referrers mechanisms. These facilities can carry checkpoint payloads without defining their execution-state semantics. OCI artifact guidance, OCI distribution specification. The checkpoint-specific OCI image proposal, issue #962, remains open. Podman can create checkpoint images, checkpointctl can build OCI-compatible images from checkpoint archives, and containerd has its own checkpoint media types. These are existing packaging practices alongside an unresolved proposal for a common definition. Registry storage alone does not establish restore compatibility across runtimes or GPU environments. Checkpoint image proposal, checkpointctl, containerd media types. Directions being explored The roadmaps cover several remaining costs. vLLM’s Fast Start work includes weight-cache validation, tuning, process startup, profiling, and graph-capture questions. SGLang’s Fast Engine Recovery roadmap includes broader model coverage, memory transport, daemon lifecycle, and initialization beyond weight loading. Their task lists describe directions; individual implementations carry their own status and supported configurations. Snapshot lifecycle proposals also explore how applications report that capture is safe and how they learn that restoration has completed. The Snapshot project’s application-hooks design discusses files, HTTP, and Unix signals for these transitions. The framework proposals approach the same boundary from the engine side. Their existence does not establish a shared protocol already adopted across projects. Application lifecycle hooks proposal. At the platform and runtime layers, ongoing work concerns Pod and GPU contracts, checkpoint artifacts, and compatibility. For readers following this area, the useful questions remain concrete: which work is preserved, which component owns it, what restoration still requires, and which environments the implementation supports. Further reading vLLM Fast Start roadmap: the direction beyond weight loading, including tuning, initialization, and validation. SGLang Fast Engine Recovery roadmap: weight-cache evolution and other startup costs under discussion. vLLM initialized-engine snapshot design: capture boundaries, compatibility checks, and restoration validation. External checkpoint orchestration RFC: proposed responsibilities of the inference engine and the external orchestrator. OCI checkpoint image definition proposal: artifact layout, metadata, and interoperability questions. Kubernetes Checkpoint Restore Working Group: community scope, meeting notes, and entry points for following platform work.

title: [CNCF] kpt v1.0.0 is released
summary: After many years and much development, the kpt community has released v1.0.0 of the kpt toolchain. This is a big step in maturing the kpt project after having it in pre-release status for several years. In the last twelve months the community has focused on stabilising the APIs, deprecating unused features and integrating the Porch (Package ORCHestration) service back into the kpt organization. With the complete toolchain under a common governance the community delivers a comprehensive system for GitOps based package management, which is modular enough to integrate and add value to any workflow. Standalone kpt provides lightweight configuration package management for applications running on Kubernetes, based on the config as data principles. These principles allow declarative manipulation and verification of the configuration of cloud native applications, clusters or indeed any resources managed through Kubernetes APIs. In kpt everything is expressed using KRM and kpt provides a framework to describe the manipulation and validation steps for KRM resources in a package, autonomously converting generic KRM into deployable models for a specific site or application. This allows reproducible KRM resource manipulation without the limitations of templating. Porch provides a framework to support the orchestration of kpt packages at scale in a zero-touch GitOps workflow. With the recent release of version 1.0.0, the kpt community is announcing the readiness of kpt for widespread adoption, having demonstrated that all the components of the project are stable and the community is actively working to build a simple, comprehensive, lightweight and modular framework for the lifecycle management of any Kubernetes resources. Join us! The kpt project meets weekly, on Wednesdays at 2pm CET. We use GitHub to collaborate on issues and discussions and we use the kpt channel on the Kubernetes slack for ad hoc communication. If what you see interests you and you would like to know more, please reach out. If you are already using kpt and would like to see a new feature, or want to help improve it, please reach out – we would be delighted to see you!

title: [Slack Engineering] Agentic Testing: Where Agents Fit in the E2E Testing Stack
summary: Abstract Agent-driven end-to-end (E2E) tests add a new exploratory layer to testing, but should they replace traditional deterministic tests? We ran more than 200 agentic E2E workflows using the Playwright MCP, Playwright CLI, and agent-generated Playwright tests in test workspaces using non-production data to find out how agentic testing could fit into both our and your testing stacks. 1. From Journeys to Goals Traditional end-to-end tests validate a specific journey through the UI. click → click → type → assert Agent-driven tests instead validate whether a goal can be achieved, often expressed as an instruction (e.g. “send a thread message”): goal → agent adapts → verify result This difference can be summarized simply: Tests enforce journeys. Agents verify goals. Across our agentic test runs, the overall workflow remained consistent (e.g. login → search → result → clear), but the exact sequence of actions varied. In practice, agents took different paths to reach the same outcome: Different input methods (clicking a search suggestion vs pressing Enter) Different navigation patterns (reopening search vs reusing existing state) Additional or skipped steps (extra clicks, snapshots, or intermediate actions) Agents can still validate intermediate steps when needed, but this flexibility comes with tradeoffs in reliability, cost, and execution time, which we explore in the next sections. The Problem Agent-driven E2E testing looks promising, but it raises a real question: can something that costs $15–30 per run and takes over 10 minutes actually fit into modern testing workflows? At first glance, the answer seems like no. But in 200+ runs, we found they are fundamentally different from traditional tests. They can be highly reliable and have a clear place in the testing stack. This is largely due to recent advances in large language models, which enable agents to write code, debug failures, and interact directly with user interfaces. These capabilities introduce a new execution model for testing, but where they fit in existing E2E workflows is not always clear. 2. Our Experiment To understand how agent-driven tests can fit into E2E workflows, we ran 200+ automated executions across multiple configurations to measure reliability, execution speed, and cost. Execution models We evaluated three different approaches: Agent + Playwright MCP The agent interacts with the browser through the Playwright MCP, using predefined browser actions (clicking elements, typing input, reading DOM state, etc…) with persistent context (DOM snapshots and logs) Agent + Playwright CLI The agent interacts with the browser by running Playwright CLI commands via the shell, executing one step at a time and deciding the next action based on the updated UI state Generated Playwright Tests An AI agent generates deterministic Playwright test code from a natural language description, executes it as a standard E2E test, and iteratively refines it until it passes Experiment Setup Agent model (Playwright MCP / CLI): Claude Sonnet 4.5 Model used for generated Playwright tests: Claude Opus 4.6 Execution: non-interactive Claude Code (claude -p) Browser tooling: Playwright MCP Playwright CLI Environment setup: Slack Dev API MCP All experiments were conducted in test workspaces using non-production data Test flows We used two flows to cover different levels of complexity. These flows were kept consistent across all experiments to allow for direct comparison. Thread Reply (simple) A shorter workflow (~15–20 steps) involving creating a channel, sending a message, replying in a thread, and verifying thread state Search Discovery (medium complexity) A longer workflow (~25–30 steps) involving entering search queries, navigating results, moving between views (search, channels, threads), and verifying expected outcomes Input formats For agent-driven approaches, we evaluated two input types: Natural language (NL) Detailed, human-readable instructions describing the workflow and expected outcomes (e.g. “reply in a thread, and verify it appears in All Threads”), often written as step-by-step lists Structured YAML The same workflow expressed in a structured format, with explicit steps, actions, targets, and expected outcomes The difference is not the level of detail, but how that detail is represented: natural language requires the agent to interpret and map instructions to actions, while YAML defines that mapping more explicitly. Each configuration was run 20 times. The experiment matrix below shows the full setup: Experiment Matrix Exp Execution Model Input Type Tools Thread Reply Search Discovery 1 Agent (Playwright MCP) NL MCP 20 20 2 Agent (Playwright MCP) YAML MCP 20 20 3 Agent (Playwright CLI) NL CLI 20 20 4 Agent (Playwright CLI) YAML CLI 20 20 5 Agent (Generated Tests) NL Code 20 20 3. What We Observed Summary of Results Before diving into individual metrics, here’s a quick look at how the different approaches performed overall across both natural language and YAML-based executions. Approach Failure rate (thread reply) Failure rate (search discovery) Avg runtime Agent (Playwright MCP) 0% ~12% ~5–8 min Agent (Playwright CLI) ~12% ~20% ~9–11 min Generated Playwright Tests ~8% ~48% ~3 min The following sections break down these results by individual metrics. Reliability One of the clearest patterns we saw was how reliability changed as flows became more complex. Across the agentic Playwright flows, the Playwright MCP was the more reliable configuration, consistently achieving near‑zero failure rates on simple scenarios and remaining within 0–12% on more complex flows. In contrast, the Playwright CLI showed higher failure rates (roughly 12–20%), with many failures caused by execution issues such as authentication handling, navigation timing, and session instability rather than model reasoning. Generated Playwright tests performed reasonably well on simple flows (~8% failure rate), but degraded significantly on more complex workflows (~48%). These tests were not entirely wrong, as they typically progressed through 70-80% of the flow before breaking on a final interaction or assertion. Failures were primarily caused by variability in UI state and abstraction mismatches. These tests were generated from loosely specified natural language flows and reused existing page object abstractions, which sometimes interfered with precise element targeting in more complex scenarios. Overall, the reliability gap widened with increasing complexity, suggesting that the agent-native execution models like MCP provide more stable behavior as flows get harder. One likely reason is how each model handles state. MCP keeps a live, stable view of the app, while CLI rebuilds state from snapshots at each step. As flows get longer, small inconsistencies in how the UI is interpreted or timed can accumulate and lead to failures. Another likely factor is in-session context. In MCP-based runs, the agent appears to reuse successful interactions from earlier steps in the same flow, while CLI can feel more like starting from scratch at each step. We didn’t explicitly measure this, but it may also contribute to the gap. Speed When it came to speed, generated tests were consistently the fastest. Approach Average Duration Generated Playwright Tests ~3 minutes Agent (Playwright MCP) ~5–8 minutes Agent (Playwright CLI) ~9–11 minutes For generated tests, the runtime includes both test generation and execution. Each test was generated once and executed five times, and the numbers above reflect the average duration per run. In practice, the raw execution was much faster: ~32 seconds for thread reply and ~45 seconds for search discovery. In CI environments where tests run repeatedly, the one-time generation cost becomes negligible, allowing deterministic tests to scale more efficiently. Agent-driven workflows pay this cost on every run. Each step typically involves: Observing the UI state Reasoning about the next action Executing the action and validating the result Adaptability Another pattern we saw was how differently agents navigate the UI. Only about 20% of runs followed the exact same sequence of actions. In most runs, the agent discovered different valid UI paths to reach the same goal. For example, while still reaching the same final state, the agent might: Open menus in a different order Select slightly different UI elements Use alternate navigation flows To measure this, we compared action signatures across runs. An action signature is the ordered list of tool calls and UI actions performed by the agent (e.g. API calls, browser clicks, form interactions). Action signatures were normalized before comparison: parameters, wait/snapshot actions, and equivalent tool variants (e.g. fill vs type) were collapsed so that only meaningful differences in the action sequence were counted. Across runs, most action sequences differed even when the final outcome was correct. This highlights a key difference between approaches: traditional E2E tests enforce a single deterministic journey through the UI, while agents explore the interface and verify whether the goal state can still be reached. Cost and Where It Comes From Cost stood out in our experiments. Agent-driven runs were typically $15–30 per execution, compared to much cheaper traditional test runs. To understand where this cost came from, we analyzed token usage across different execution models by running the same search discovery flow. Approach Tokens MCP (Opus 4.6) ~3.8M MCP (Sonnet 4.5) ~3.5M MCP (Haiku 4.5) ~5.7M CLI (Opus 4.6) ~6M Code Gen (Opus 4.6) ~7M The first thing that stood out was that how the agent was executed mattered more than which model powered it. Haiku did use more tokens than Sonnet or Opus in our runs, but all of the MCP-based approaches still used fewer tokens overall than the CLI and Code Gen approaches for the same flow. To understand why, we looked at how Claude Code executes agent sessions. The underlying API is stateless and every turn re-sends the full system prompt plus the entire conversation history. This means cost is not driven by model output, which is negligible, but by how quickly context accumulates and how many turns the agent takes to complete the flow. Approach Turns MCP (Opus 4.6) ~40 MCP (Sonnet 4.5) ~40 MCP (Haiku 4.5) ~60 CLI (Opus 4.6) ~85 Code Gen (Opus 4.6) ~70 On average, CLI took 85 turns compared to MCP’s ~40-60 because each browser interaction was split across multiple commands, such as actions, waits, snapshots, reads, and element lookups. MCP combined interaction and state return into a single round trip. Each additional turn pays the full system prompt tax plus re-sends all prior conversation context. What fills that context? For MCP and CLI approaches, browser snapshots are the primary payload. Playwright MCP returns accessibility tree snapshots as part of its browser interaction responses, and these accumulate in the conversation window across all subsequent turns. For Code Gen, the accumulated context comes from test runner output containing full error traces, assertion failures, and DOM state on each retry cycle. In our analysis, the majority of the cost was retransmission of previously seen content. Only a small fraction of tokens represented new information per turn. The biggest factors affecting cost are turn count and context growth rate rather than model reasoning or output generation. At this stage, we focused primarily on reliability and behavior, so token usage was not optimized. Opportunities to reduce cost include prompt caching, context compaction, and reducing snapshot frequency. Due to the cost, agent-driven testing may currently be better suited for targeted debugging or exploratory testing than for high-frequency CI execution, although cost may improve with future models and tooling. Infrastructure Matters (MCP vs CLI) Another important takeaway was how much the execution environment affected reliability, not just the model itself. Approach Failure rate Agent (Playwright MCP) 0–12% Agent (Playwright CLI) 12–20% Most failures in CLI-based runs came from authentication and navigation issues (sign-in errors, timeouts, and session instability), suggesting that many failures were caused by the execution layer rather than the agent’s reasoning. The Playwright MCP provides structured browser primitives and tighter integration with the agent’s tool-calling workflow, while CLI-based execution introduces additional layers between the agent and the browser. Parallelization also differed. MCP runs were easy to execute concurrently, while CLI-based runs were difficult to parallelize in our setup and were mostly executed sequentially. These results suggest that reliability, speed, and cost depend not just on the model, but also on how stable and well-designed the execution environment is. Execution Capability Boundaries Our experiments focused on single-session UI workflows. More complex scenarios, such as cross-workspace flows or workflows that open multiple browser windows, introduce a different set of challenges where the choice of execution model may matter as much as the agent itself. Both MCP and CLI-based approaches could support these workflows, but with different tradeoffs. MCP may run into cost issues as observation loops grow over longer flows, while CLI-based approaches may introduce additional coordination complexity when managing multiple browser sessions, on top of the higher token usage observed in our experiments. We did not explore these scenarios here, but they are an important consideration for teams evaluating agent-driven testing. 4. Where Agentic Testing Fits in the Testing Pyramid So where does agent-driven testing actually fit? Rather than replacing existing approaches, it adds a new capability on top of them. Deterministic E2E Tests Best suited for fast, repeatable regression checks in CI. Human-written or AI-generated tests Fast, repeatable, and CI-friendly Low operational cost Enforce a specific journey through the UI Agentic Testing Agent-driven workflows operate differently from deterministic tests. Instead of executing a predefined script, agents operate from a goal: they observe the UI, reason about the current state, and determine how to reach the desired outcome. Exploring complex UI behavior Debugging flaky workflows Reproducing production bugs Testing Pyramid with Agentic Layer Testing pyramid with four layers: Unit Tests, Integration Tests, E2E Testing, and Agentic Testing From a system perspective, agentic testing still operates at the same level as E2E tests, validating real user workflows through the UI. The difference is in how those workflows are executed. For this reason, the most effective testing strategies of the future will combine both. Deterministic tests provide a stable foundation for CI, while agentic testing adds a distinct layer at the top of the testing pyramid for exploration, debugging, and validating complex behaviors. 5. That foundation made it much easier to run, analyze, and iterate on hundreds of executions. Special thanks to our managers, Dave Harrington and Vani Anantha, for supporting experiments at a scale that definitely kept the token counters busy, and briefly put us on our internal token usage leaderboard. We also want to thank the Frontend Test Frameworks team for their help throughout the process, from early ideas to validation and feedback.
